title: After 11 month of building, I'm open-sourcing my game engine built for AI art and coding agents.
author: dilum14
selftext:
My hope with this set of tools is to make building games fun. I wanted to see how much boring stuff I could remove so devs can enjoy making games and focus more on the fun stuff like the gameplay/story etc. This isn't a perfect solution, it's more of a first genuine attempt. (You'll be surprised how far you can go.)
    
    
    Below are the three things I'm sharing today.
    
    
    1. A game engine built for AI-generated assets and coding agents
    
    
    Supports 2D top-down games (Stardew-style perspective with two-directional sprites). Four-directional character sprites are coming soon.
    
    
    2. An asset generation MCP that outputs game objects, not just PNGs
    
    
    This is the part that saved me the most time. It handles the structuring you'd normally have to do by hand:
    
    
    - Maps generated with bounding boxes, depth masks, and obstacle masks that work out of the box.
    - Characters and props with strict style consistency across outfit and tool variations, plus prop sequences like crop lifecycles.
    - VFX for interactive state transitions with animation (e.g. a fire pit), plus overlay props for transitions without animation (e.g. opening a door).
    - A HUD that ships with an HTML overlay (coordinates and placeholders) so your agent can wire up click events quickly.
    - Background music. (The background music in the video was generated with this.)
    
    
    3. A server SDK for the boring parts
    
    
    Player accounts, cloud saves, and multiplayer in one or two lines. Free to use just ask your agent to set it up.
    
    
    The demo is a step-by-step walkthrough using Sonnet 4.5 on purpose a weaker model so you can see the floor. The art is rough, and still you see the engine pulling through and things like y sorting and consistent overlays etc.
    
    
    Transparency:
    
    
    - The engine is open source.
    - The MCP is available and runs at cost, so you only pay for the API and the GPU costs, there's no profit margin.
    - The SDK is shipped and free, but it's not open source yet since it's still buried in my codebase. I'll open-source it as soon as possible and update the pricing details then.
    
    
    Keeping this post clean to follow the sub's rules. Drop a comment, and I'll DM you the GitHub repo, MCP setup, and Discord invite.

comments.author: brother_spirit
comments.body:
I have a similar concept for this I made so that people with low technical skill or intellectual impairments could do game development.  
It worked/works amazingly well actually - far better than I hoped.  
The concept is simply have a 3D engine (I used an OSS three.js shooter engine) + an asset library + map building tools available to a chat embedded chat agent you call through the API.  
The chat agent has a pre-made JSON schema it can plug natural language requests into and hot load the game.  
So you can say "spawn a car i front of me" and the game hot loads a car.  
"Make it purple" and the game knows you meant the car, turns it purple.   
"Now cover the sky in flames and make my AK-47 an umbrella" changes the sky texture map and weapon model, etc.

replies.author: dilum14
replies.body: That's a pretty neat idea ngl

replies.author: brother_spirit
replies.body:
I would love nothing more than for someone to take it and make it a reality.

I tried to get funding to build a program around it from my boss but didn't get much interest. 

It's the kind of concept that probably just scales with model intelligence; it really doesn't matter what SOTA is, Fable is unlikely to be used by a beginner/learner for "real time" A, B, C type game development work, but the cheap little Haikui/whatever model plugged into taht Three.JS engine can just just work forever for next to nothing. To make it "better" you can just use the SOTA models to develop the game systems/assets it's calling through it's JSON schema 

I've almost talked myself into starting it back up again with Fable 👀

replies.author: dilum14
replies.body: This is actually a cool idea. I find that if the speed is there, people might enjoy it. The thing I wasn't sure about is how much variance there is, since you said it has a prebuilt system, wouldn't that limit the gameplay? That's one of the things I focused on with my engine, where people can extend it to anything.

replies.author: brother_spirit
replies.body:
Basically, yes. "In world" swapping actions like "Make my RPG be an umbrella that shoots watermelons" requires both an Umbrella 3D asset and an RPG asset available in library. However, the model can "improvise" and use similar assets with an apology given (for example it may substitute in a beach ball for the Watermelon because it has that available and reasons it will still be in line with the intention of the request).   
And then "range of motion" in game - how to place an object, create a collider, , modify physics, etc are "pre-determined" via the systems and the JSON Schema in the engine.  
The basic idea is; you really don't need "infinite" possibility.  
Literally just asset swapping + object loading + map system + enemies placing/logic gives you the ability to make shooters, movements games, etc.

The procedural map placement having proper colliders, interior/ext transitions was where I was up to and was proving to be the tricky bit but to be honest that was working with Sonnet 4.5 many months ago. Given the Three.js engine is so incredibly small I really don't see why any sort of procedural system is out of scope for an agent.

replies.author: dilum14
replies.body: I see. Do you have any examples you've built? I would love to try out some. So my intentions with this game engine are for people to build commercial games, which is why I wanted to go full on generative with no restrictions except the camera angle for now. But I think you said your intentions were more for beginners, friendly, right

replies.author: brother_spirit
replies.body:
I don't have any footage but it has basic movement, shooting, guns, enemies, weapon swapping, object summoning. I was mid-way through making "custom reload animation system" where a goofy object like an Umbrella gets a logical anchor point assigned and then run through a default motion tween to replicate a shot gun pump. Lol. At the moment you can just hold the prop like a gun and I just want generalizaed procedural systems for the agent to use.   
It has a chat window always available. "Give me zero gravity" let's you fly, etc. "Make it moon grav now" gives you half gravity.   


And yes - very much aimed at an  ultra beginner. The intention is to make game development incredibly easy and approachable for someone with an intellectual impairment. By pre-building friendly generative systems + an asset library and a cheap yet capable model to interact with they can do "slice by slice" gave dev with very simple and basic requests. The system also tracks "learning" of concepts and tries to scaffold the learner less over time or increase concept depth and verbosity when communicating in response to learning. 

Of course they could just do the same thing with Fable but the API costs would be insane. Haiku with the right tools is honeslty perfectly capable at driving the engine and costs like... 0.025 to 0.05 cents per prompt? Something like that - I spend weeks working on it and used like a dollar or two of API credits

comments.author: susimposter6969
comments.body: is there a reason you didn't just bolt this on to an existing open source engine

replies.author: dilum14
replies.body:
Great question! There are two main areas I wanted to focus on.

The first is treating AI-generated images as first-class citizens. Most traditional game engines are built around grid- or block-based systems designed for human-authored art and procedural generation. This engine takes the opposite approach. Since AI image models are trained to generate complete images, there is no need to impose rigid structures and lose natural elements like shadows and lighting that we get for free. Instead, the engine uses AI art as-is, making flat 2D images playable and interactive, while supporting features like depth sorting by default to give the 3d feel.

The second focus is optimizing for coding agents and context efficiency. The engine follows an architecture of simple interfaces with deep modules and minimal external dependencies. If you look at the configuration, it mostly relies on development dependencies for features like hot reloading and TypeScript support. This ensures the engine doesn't restrict what you can do; every file is editable, allowing coding agents to work without constraints. However, because coding agents can quickly make a codebase messy, I have embedded skills and recipes directly inside the repository. This allows the agents to look up documentation and follow clean design patterns automatically.

Finally, using HTML5 and TypeScript provides unique advantages when working with AI. Because coding agents are heavily trained on web codebases, that training transfers directly to this engine. This means even an off-the-shelf, open-source model can assist in building games much more easily. Furthermore, since HTML5 is a standard web technology, it is supported across almost all major platforms. This makes it simple to deploy your games to mobile, desktop, or virtually any operating system that supports web standards, with very few exceptions.

Hope this makes sense!

comments.author: tinyDevBigQuest
comments.body: This looks really impressive. I’m actually more curious about the asset generation MCP than the engine itself. How are you generating the characters, sprite animations, maps, etc behind the scenes?  Also, are you planning to open-source any part of the MCP or could you share more details about the generation pipeline?

replies.author: dilum14
replies.body: Hey, thanks for the question! Each asset has different workflows around it. For most things, I first run an enhancer step to take a query and sort of ground it with the camera angle, etc., as just a prompt. Then, usually it's an image generation api, after that, I have a couple of segmentation models trained to segment things and add that metadata layer, for instance, a map. I have three models, one segmenting obstacles like the (eg, barn), and then another takes the segment and then extracts the colliders. The engine is required to turn this metadata and make it useful. Regarding the open sourcing of the MCP, it's not just workflows; then I need to open-source the segmentation models and everything to make it useful, and these models need substantial GPUs, like, for example, I'm running on Nvidia T4S. If you wanna try this approach, you can check out, for example, sam-3.1, which is an open source model for segmentation; it wasn't reliable enough for me; it's like a hit or miss type of thing.

comments.author: ap0ught
comments.body:
I'm gonna fork the repo and take a look later on. But my initial thoughts without looking at it is by putting the code inside of the engine itself. You are interacting with the engine by making queries. And someone else is interacting with the engine by using the same queries. the ones. But the engine can evolve and become smarter. So when the third person interacts with the engine, they're not starting from scratch.
Then you can have a person that looks at how the developers or designers are interacting with the engine and they can streamline that process so it's cleaner.

To take the example from higher up, if you want something that will go behind the building, then the engine will know that trees don't normally move, so they don't have to have a layer associated with them. But people or pigs will.
